questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: My erasmus exchange in Belgium was a unique opportunity because of the courses in translation and interpretation offered at UMONS that cannot be found in Denmark in the same context. It was also important for me that my study language french was spoken at the destination of my erasmus, and I was very interested in exploring another francophone culture than the one in France.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I had trouble finding information about my courses and where I had to be at campus. However, my teachers and fellow students were very helpful, and everything worked out in the end.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The erasmus responsable teacher at my host university met with me before the semester started and showed me around the campus. She also helped me change my LA with recommended changes and schedule-coordination. There were several events for erasmus students where we got a lot of useful information about municipal registration, student activities, classes, etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy, as the host university sent out an email with a few recommended websites for student accommodation in the city. The websites were easy to manage and I quickly got in contact with a private house owner with an available room.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: They should be prepared that private housing has its pros and cons. It can be less formal than university housing, but also provided less assistance and can cause trouble because owner/tenant relationship is different in a foreign country than in ones home country. I had trouble with my landlord because I thought I could be familiar with him when a problem occured, but one should have in mind that belgians are very formal and serious in non-familiar situations, such as one between a landlord and a tenant. With the university, everything is very clear and it is hard to fall out with a landlord because it's such a big and organized organisation.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are a lot of student housings in the city, either big apartment buildings (usually university housing) or old city houses with 3-10 students. I knew erasmus students in university housing and private housing that experienced pros and cons with both housings.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process was quite confusing. My host university has a lot of small courses from 2 to 5 ECTS per course, and many of them overlap. You can't be sure that you will be able to follow all of your courses from your original LA. Apparently this is not only for erasmus students.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The doors to the secretariat were always open and the secretaries could always help. I also had a lot of help from my teachers and fellow students.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I could registrate for approx. 30% of the courses in my original LA, but the new courses that I was recommended to replace the last 70% were much better, I think.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't lock yourself onto the courses that you chose before going on your exchange. They will most likely have to be replaced because of schedule changes, a level too low or too high or that the course won't even be offered that semester. Keep an open mind and don't be afraid to ask for help, because you will definitely need it. Find out who is qualified to recommend courses for your particular academic profile.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: All of my courses was in MA level, except for one course that was in BA and one course that was for erasmus students in general.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching at UMONS is definitely more practical, whereas it's much more (if not exclusively) theoretical at UCPH. This makes sense because the courses at UMONS prepare you for a very practical job, namely translation and interpretation. Personally I much rather prefer the style of teaching at UMONS, especially because it's so speech-oriented, you spend a lot of time practicing the studied language. In UCPH we spend a lot of time studying french in danish, and reading a lot of fictional literature. In my erasmus exchange, my speech qualifications and vocabulary has developped more than it has in three years.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: French as a Foreign Language, Introduction to translation, Translation DA-FR, Translation FR-DA, Consecutive Interpretation DA-FR, Consecutive Interpretation FR-DA, Simultaneous interpretation, Liaison-interpretation, Translation Workshop.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: All of the above. If you are interested in translation and interpretation in French-Danish, these give you a great introduction to the subject. However, the master-courses are a bit tough in the beginning for someone who has never tried interpretation before. The other students in the master already have some theory in the baggage from the bachelor. But the teachers are really good and they will help you as much as you need, so it's really doable.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You have to pay 5 euros to register your address in Mons at the local foreigners' office and they require passport photos which will cost an additional 8 euros in the supermarket, if you don't already have some. You also have to report to the foreigners' office when you want to cancel your address in Mons, but you can do that by mail so you avoid paying 5 euros again.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Grocery shopping in the city was a lot more expensive than I had imagined, even being aware of the inflation.
Beer is cheaper than soda.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were a lot of student activities at the university, either free/open ones or where you had to sign up. However, to join a sports team it was a complicated process because you had to sign up on some kind of website, buy a sports card somewhere, sign up to the classes.. It was just a bit too confusing so I ended up not signing up for anything. I went running in nature instead.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were traditional competitions such as; cart race, the mons cup (football), cheerleading, and more. There were also cultural activities like different concerts and La Journée Internationale where students from all departments at the EII-FTI faculty had prepared food and decorations from the country whose language they were studying. I know there were also several athletic activities but I never really looked into it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you go in the spring semester, definitely go see the cheerleading competition. It means a lot to a lot of UMONS-students and they really make a big deal out of it! Besides, it's a great opportunity to get to know some belgians students over a few beers. Make sure to also join the Journée Internationale at EII-FTI, especially if you study at that faculty, and make sure to cook something from your home country - your department will be able to sell a lot more tickets if they can tell people that a real person from that country made this dish.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Definitely visit other cities in Belgium, both in Wallonia and Flanders. It's an interesting country with a lot of ancient towns with beautiful architecture and a lot of cultural and lingual diversity. Belgium is also located in the heart of Europe, so you can travel to many interesting places around Central Europe, only 1 to 4 hours from Brussels.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was not that complicated, as the belgian culture in Mons is quite similar to french culture because of the town's proximity to the french border, and I've already lived in France before so I am familiar with this culture. However, Belgians are very subtle and indirect, more than Danes. Therefore I had to tone down my excitement and energy level a bit to adapt to my surroundings (but maybe that's just me as a person).

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to approach the local students, even if they don't approach you first. They may seem shy at first, but they will embrace you once you get to know them a bit. The best way to socialize with local students is if you both have a beer in your hand.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Belgians don't talk about they're feeling so much. From a Dane's point of view, I found them a bit cold and uninterested at first and it took me a while to figure out that they are not insensitive, they are just a bit less intimate with people who are not their partner.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Once you are friends with a belgian, you will always be. They are super friendly and open, and they will welcome you any time. They are also not pompous and they are very open to foreign cultures.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) Be prepared to change your LA 2) Your french level is going to improve A LOT 3) it is easy only to hang out with other erasmus students, but try to get to know belgian students as well. It is a great way to be more familiar with the university and the belgian culture.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: 99% of the streets in the city are made with paving stones, and they are rough to walk on. So bring practical everyday shoes, and leave the heels at home!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part of my exchange was my classes and the encouragement from my teachers. I found a new interest for interpretation and translation that I wouldn't have gotten if I had stayed at my home university. I got the chance to visit the interpreters and translators at the EU institutions (EU Court of Justice and EU-Commission) and I strongly consider pursuing interpretation as a profession.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I found that I was usually the oldest person in the company when socializing with other erasmus students or even local students (except the one other student in my master classes). It could be challenging at times, as I was occasionally missing the company of people my own age or older, but it was not a crucial problem at all.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Erasmus exchange is one of the best decisions any university student could ever make. I highly recommend it, regardless if it's in Belgium or any other country.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
